message.content:
The sea’s “color” isn’t fixed—it varies with many factors:

| Factor | Typical Appearance |
|--------|--------------------|
| **Depth** | Shallow waters often look bright turquoise or aqua because they reflect sunlight strongly. Deeper water absorbs longer wavelengths (red/orange) first, leaving mostly short‑wave blue/green hues. At extreme depths it can appear almost black. |
| **Clarity / Turbidity** | Clear water scatters less light, so you see deeper into the blue spectrum. Murky or algae‑rich water may shift toward greens or even brownish tones. |
| **Sun Angle & Time of Day** | Early morning or late afternoon sun gives warmer, golden glows over waves. Noon tends to show crisp blues. |
| **Surface Conditions** | Calm surfaces produce smooth reflections of the sky, while rough seas scatter light more diffusely, giving a richer, darker tone. |

So most people describe open ocean as *blue*—often a vivid azure or teal—but depending on conditions it can range from pale turquoise to dark indigo, occasionally shifting toward green or gray when influenced by sediments, plankton, or atmospheric effects.
